children: California's legislature has approved a first-of-its-kind state law setting rules for how lawyers are permitted to use generative artificial intelligence in their work.
Both chambers in the California legislature approved the current version of the measure as of Monday. The bill, SB 574, now goes to Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom to sign or veto.
Newsom's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday.

Lawyers across the country are increasingly using AI tools in legal practice. In a growing number of cases, judges have sanctioned litigants for including erroneous or made-up AI-generated material in court filings without verifying the output.

Under California's measure, a lawyer "shall not delegate the practice of law" to generative AI. Lawyers would be required to take "reasonable steps" to verify the accuracy of all materials produced using AI, including case citations, and correct any false or hallucinated output in any AI-generated material they use.

Lawyers also would be required to disclose the use of AI for documents submitted in court and would be barred from entering confidential or other nonpublic information into certain generative AI systems. Arbitrators under the bill also could not delegate any decision-making to an AI tool.

Senator Tom Umberg, a Democrat who chairs the California Senate's judiciary committee, introduced the bill. He told Reuters on Tuesday that lawyers continue to "submit materials that have hallucinations or have some other anomaly, and they attribute it to AI, and that simply can't exist."
"Our system, our courts, our judiciary has to rely on the integrity of the litigants and the advocates. And if they can't do that, everything breaks down," he said.

The bill builds on requirements that already bind lawyers under state rules governing civil litigation, such as the need for court filings to be supported by existing law. It was modeled after a separate California rule for the use of AI by judges and court employees adopted by the California Judicial Council.
The Judicial Council, the policy-making body for the state's court system, said it has no position or comment on the legislation.

The requirement to verify all material submitted in court "should raise the standard for lawyers," Umberg said. The measure also "gives the courts another tool if lawyers don't follow the law, in terms of potential sanctions," he said.
Some lawyers in California have said the law in part mirrors obligations that attorneys in the state already must obey.

Wayne Stacy, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Technology at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, said the measure is largely "duplicative" of existing ethics rules covering lawyers.
